Feldspar. The most abundant mineral in Earth's crust, comprising about sixty percent of all igneous rocks. It's an aluminosilicate mineral that forms at high temperatures, and it's the primary component of granitic and basaltic rocks. Feldspars weather readily, breaking down into clay minerals that form the foundation of soils.

Feldspars are rated six to six point five on the Mohs scale, softer than quartz but harder than calcite. In igneous rocks, they form blocky crystals and easily cleave along planes due to their internal structure. There are two main groups. Orthoclase is potassium-rich and found in granites. Plagioclase is sodium and calcium-rich and found in basalts. Over geological time, feldspars weather more readily than quartz, releasing silica and breaking down into clay and feldspar sand.

Industrially, feldspar is used in ceramics, glass manufacture, and as a flux in metalworking. It's a primary mineral in granite, alongside quartz and mica. Plagioclase feldspar is the dominant mineral in basaltic lava flows. In most igneous rocks, feldspar is a companion mineral to quartz, though quartz is harder and more chemically stable. Feldspars are also often found alongside mica in granites and metamorphic rocks, and they're silicate minerals with the addition of aluminium, making them fundamental to the mineral landscape.
